title: OA 4 — Time Series and Quantitative Analytics
description: Mock data-science internship assessment: time-series validation and forecast errors, PCA and clustering, bootstrap, ANOVA, regression diagnostics, neural-network basics; price/benchmark SQL (Securities / DailyPrices / SectorMap / Benchmarks); resampling and rolling analytics in pandas; dynamic-programming and binary-search DSA.
disclaimer: Independent practice material informed by publicly reported role requirements and general internship-assessment patterns. Not official Nasdaq questions.

revealPolicy.rule: Never send private fields to the candidate's browser; reveal solutions only after the whole attempt has been submitted or timed out.

questions.statement: You are forecasting next-day volatility from three years of daily data. Which validation scheme is most appropriate for choosing hyper-parameters?

options.text: Train on the most recent year and test on the oldest year
Validate on the training data, since time series are autocorrelated
Standard shuffled 5-fold cross-validation, because it uses all data efficiently
Walk-forward (expanding or rolling window) validation: always train on the past and validate on a later block

solution.explanation: Shuffled folds put future observations in the training set and past ones in validation, leaking information and giving optimistic scores. Walk-forward validation mimics production: only past data can be used to predict the future.

questions.statement: A forecast has errors (actual − forecast) of 2, −2, 2 and −10 over four days. Which pair of statements is correct?

options.text: MAE = 4 and RMSE ≈ 5.29; RMSE is larger because it penalises the large error more
MAE ≈ 5.29 and RMSE = 4
MAE = 4 and RMSE = 4; the two metrics are always equal
MAE = 0 because positive and negative errors cancel

solution.explanation: MAE = (2+2+2+10)/4 = 4. RMSE = √((4+4+4+100)/4) = √28 ≈ 5.29. Squaring weights big errors more, so RMSE ≥ MAE with equality only if all absolute errors are equal. The mean of signed errors (the bias) is 0 here, which is not MAE.

questions.statement: A PCA on standardised returns of 10 stocks gives eigenvalues 6, 3, 1 (and zeros for the remaining components). What fraction of total variance is explained by the first two principal components?

solution.explanation: Explained variance ratio = (6 + 3)/(6 + 3 + 1) = 0.9. The first component alone explains 60%.

questions.statement: After clustering stocks with k-means, a point has a silhouette value of −0.4. What does this indicate?

options.text: The point is exactly on the cluster centroid
The point is perfectly clustered
The point is on average closer to the points of a neighbouring cluster than to its own cluster, so it is probably misassigned
The clustering algorithm failed to run

solution.explanation: Silhouette s = (b − a)/max(a, b), where a is the mean distance to its own cluster and b the mean distance to the nearest other cluster. Values near +1 mean well clustered; negative values mean b < a.

questions.statement: While training a neural network the loss oscillates wildly and sometimes becomes NaN after a few iterations. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: The labels are balanced; remove half of them
The learning rate is too small; increase it by 100×
The model has too few parameters; add more epochs
The learning rate is too large; reduce it (and/or clip gradients)

solution.explanation: A too-large step overshoots minima and can blow up, giving oscillation or divergence (NaN). Reducing the learning rate or clipping gradients stabilises training.

questions.statement: A student regresses one stock's raw price level on another's raw price level (both trending random walks) and gets R² = 0.95. What is the main concern?

options.text: R² can never be that high for financial data, so the regression must be a typo
Spurious regression: non-stationary trending series can look strongly related by chance; model returns/differences or test for cointegration instead
High R² guarantees good out-of-sample forecasts
The regression proves that one stock causes the other

solution.explanation: Independent random walks frequently yield high R² and significant t-statistics because of shared trends. Differencing to obtain stationary returns (or testing for cointegration) avoids this trap; correlation in levels is not causation.

questions.statement: You want a 95% confidence interval for the median daily return from 250 observations without assuming normality. Which bootstrap procedure is correct?

options.text: Resample the 250 returns with replacement many times, compute the median of each resample, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of those medians
Take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentile of the original 250 returns
Resample once and use ±1.96 standard deviations of that sample
Sample 250 returns without replacement many times and average the medians

solution.explanation: The bootstrap approximates the sampling distribution of a statistic by resampling the data with replacement. The percentile interval of the bootstrap medians estimates uncertainty in the median; percentiles of the raw returns describe the spread of returns, not the uncertainty of the median.

questions.statement: A one-way ANOVA compares mean returns of 3 sectors with 10 stocks each. The between-group sum of squares is 30 and the within-group sum of squares is 54. What is the F statistic?

solution.explanation: df between = 3 − 1 = 2, df within = 30 − 3 = 27. MSB = 30/2 = 15, MSW = 54/27 = 2, F = 15/2 = 7.5. 15 is MSB alone; 0.56 inverts the ratio of sums of squares.

questions.statement: A plot of residuals versus fitted values from a linear regression of trading volume on market cap shows a funnel shape (spread grows with the fitted value). Which assumption is violated and what is a standard remedy?

options.text: Linearity of means only; add an intercept
Normality of the features; standardise them
Homoscedasticity (constant error variance); use a transformation such as log(volume) or heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors
Independence of features; delete the first row

solution.explanation: A funnel pattern means the error variance changes with the fitted value (heteroscedasticity). OLS coefficient estimates stay unbiased but standard errors are wrong; log transforms or robust (e.g., White) standard errors are common fixes.

questions.statement: In a simple linear regression of one stock's return on another's, the sample correlation is r = 0.8. What is R²?

solution.explanation: In simple linear regression R² = r² = 0.64: 64% of the variance of the response is explained by the predictor. √0.8 ≈ 0.89 is a common mistake.

questions.statement: Two independent assets have return variances 4 and 9 (in %²). A portfolio invests 50% in each. What is the portfolio variance?

solution.explanation: For independent assets Var = w₁²σ₁² + w₂²σ₂² = 0.25·4 + 0.25·9 = 3.25. 6.5 is the weighted-average variance; 13 simply adds the variances.

questions.statement: A weight has value 2.0, the gradient of the loss with respect to it is 0.5, and the learning rate is 0.1. After one gradient-descent step what is the weight?

solution.explanation: w ← w − η·∇L = 2.0 − 0.1·0.5 = 1.95. Gradient descent moves against the gradient.

questions.statement: In a deep network with many sigmoid layers, gradients in the earliest layers become extremely small during training. Which change most directly helps?

options.text: Use even more sigmoid layers
Remove the loss function
Set every weight to zero
Use ReLU-type activations, careful initialisation/normalisation and residual (skip) connections

solution.explanation: Sigmoid derivatives are at most 0.25, so products over many layers shrink gradients (vanishing gradients). ReLU, good initialisation, normalisation and skip connections keep gradient signals usable. Zero initialisation also makes neurons identical.

questions.statement: A hill-climbing search for a portfolio configuration keeps getting stuck in a local optimum. Which modification can help it escape?

options.text: Use a smaller neighbourhood so fewer moves are considered
Only ever accept strictly better neighbours and remove randomness completely
Stop the search after the first step
Simulated annealing or random restarts: occasionally accept worse moves or start from different points

solution.explanation: Plain hill climbing cannot leave a local optimum. Randomisation (restarts) or accepting worse moves with a decreasing probability (simulated annealing) lets the search explore other regions.

questions.statement: In reinforcement learning for trade execution, what does choosing a discount factor γ close to 0 imply?

options.text: The agent cannot learn anything
The agent ignores immediate rewards and cares only about the far future
Rewards are automatically normalised to a mean of zero
The agent is short-sighted: it mostly maximises immediate rewards and gives little weight to future rewards

solution.explanation: The return is Σ γᵗ rₜ. With γ ≈ 0 only the first terms matter. γ close to 1 values long-term outcomes (but makes learning harder).

questions.statement: You want every price row to appear together with the average close of its sector on the same row. Which construct achieves this without collapsing rows?

options.text: SELECT DISTINCT AVG(close)
HAVING AVG(close) > 0
SELECT sector, AVG(close) ... GROUP BY sector
AVG(close) OVER (PARTITION BY sector)

solution.explanation: Window aggregates compute a value over a partition but keep each input row. GROUP BY collapses rows to one per group.

questions.statement: Table A has key values 1, 2, 2, 3 and table B has key values 2, 2, 3, 4. How many rows does A LEFT JOIN B ON A.key = B.key return?

solution.explanation: Key 2 matches 2×2 = 4 row pairs, key 3 matches 1, so the inner join has 5 rows; key 1 has no match but is kept by LEFT JOIN with NULLs, giving 6. Many-to-many matches multiply rows.

It does not compile
ab
abcd

solution.explanation: Strings are immutable: `concat` returns a new String that is discarded here, so `s` still refers to "ab".

options.text: It does not compile because c is static

solution.explanation: A static field belongs to the class and is shared by all instances; each constructor call increments the same variable.

questions.statement: A function returns the rolling mean of a series for a given window size. Which test is most likely to expose an off-by-one error in how the first rolling value is produced?

options.text: A series of identical values and a window of 1
A very long random series, checking only that the function does not crash
A test that checks only the data type of the return value
A series whose length equals the window size, expecting exactly one output equal to the mean of the whole series

solution.explanation: Edge cases at the boundary between 'not enough data' and 'one full window' reveal off-by-one mistakes. Long random inputs and type checks do not pin down the first index.

questions.statement: A2:B5 contains market-cap bands sorted ascending: 0 → "Micro", 1E9 → "Small", 5E9 → "Mid", 2E10 → "Large". What does =VLOOKUP(7.5E9, A2:B5, 2, TRUE) return?

options.text: Large
Small
#N/A
Mid

solution.explanation: With approximate match (TRUE) on sorted data, VLOOKUP returns the row of the largest value less than or equal to the lookup value: 5E9 → "Mid". With FALSE it would return #N/A because 7.5E9 is not an exact key.

questions.statement: A stock's daily return standard deviation is 1.2%. Assuming independent daily returns and 252 trading days per year, what is the approximate annualised volatility?

options.text: About 1.2%
About 19.0%
About 302%
About 4.8%

solution.explanation: Volatility scales with the square root of time: 1.2% × √252 ≈ 1.2% × 15.87 ≈ 19.05%. Multiplying by 252 would wrongly scale variance-like quantities.

questions.title: January Price Range Report
questions.statement:
Using `Securities` and `DailyPrices`, build a January 2024 price-range report. Consider only rows with `price_date` from `'2024-01-01'` to `'2024-01-31'` (inclusive) and a **non-NULL** `close`.

Return one row per security with **at least 3** such rows and a minimum close above 0:

`ticker, trading_days, high_close, low_close, range_pct, high_date`

* `trading_days` – number of qualifying rows
* `high_close` / `low_close` – maximum / minimum close
* `range_pct` – `(high_close - low_close) / low_close * 100`, rounded to 2 decimals
* `high_date` – the **earliest** date on which `high_close` occurred

Sort by `range_pct` descending, then `ticker` ascending.

tables.name: DailyPrices
tables.description: One row per security per trading date.

questions.starterQuery:
SELECT s.ticker, COUNT(*) AS trading_days, MAX(p.close) AS high_close, MIN(p.close) AS low_close, 0.0 AS range_pct, '' AS high_date
FROM Securities s
JOIN DailyPrices p ON p.security_id = s.security_id
-- TODO
GROUP BY s.security_id, s.ticker;
questions.outputSpec: Columns, in order: ticker, trading_days, high_close, low_close, range_pct, high_date (text). Order: range_pct DESC, ticker ASC.

hiddenTests.description: Ties in range_pct (tie-break by ticker) and repeated highs

solution.referenceSolution:
WITH j AS (
  SELECT s.security_id, s.ticker, p.price_date, p.close
  FROM Securities s
  JOIN DailyPrices p ON p.security_id = s.security_id
  WHERE p.close IS NOT NULL
    AND p.price_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31'
),
agg AS (
  SELECT security_id, ticker, COUNT(*) AS n, MAX(close) AS hi, MIN(close) AS lo
  FROM j GROUP BY security_id, ticker
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 AND MIN(close) > 0
)
SELECT agg.ticker, agg.n AS trading_days, agg.hi AS high_close, agg.lo AS low_close,
       ROUND((agg.hi - agg.lo) * 100.0 / agg.lo, 2) AS range_pct,
       (SELECT MIN(j.price_date) FROM j WHERE j.security_id = agg.security_id AND j.close = agg.hi) AS high_date
FROM agg
ORDER BY range_pct DESC, agg.ticker ASC;
solution.explanation: Filter to non-NULL January closes, aggregate per security and keep groups via HAVING; fetch the earliest date of the maximum with a correlated subquery over the filtered rows (or a window function). BETWEEN on ISO date text is inclusive on both ends.

questions.title: Excess Return versus Sector Benchmark
questions.statement:
Compare each security's daily return with its sector benchmark using `DailyPrices`, `SectorMap` and `Benchmarks`.

* A security's **return** on a date is `close / previous_close - 1`, where `previous_close` is the close of the **previous row of that security that has a non-NULL close** (rows with NULL close are ignored entirely).
* A benchmark's return is defined the same way from `bench_close` per `sector` (ignoring NULL benchmark levels).
* A date is *comparable* when both the security and its sector benchmark have a non-NULL return on that date.

For every security with at least one comparable date return:

`security_id, sector, days, avg_excess, days_outperformed`

* `days` – number of comparable dates
* `avg_excess` – average of `(security return - benchmark return)`, rounded to 6 decimals
* `days_outperformed` – number of comparable dates on which the security return is strictly greater than the benchmark return

Sort by `avg_excess` descending, then `security_id` ascending.

tables.name: DailyPrices
tables.description: One row per security per trading date.

questions.starterQuery:
SELECT p.security_id, m.sector, COUNT(*) AS days, 0.0 AS avg_excess, 0 AS days_outperformed
FROM DailyPrices p
JOIN SectorMap m ON m.security_id = p.security_id
-- TODO: LAG-based returns for security and benchmark
GROUP BY p.security_id, m.sector;
questions.outputSpec: Columns, in order: security_id, sector, days, avg_excess, days_outperformed. Order: avg_excess DESC, security_id ASC.

publicTests.description: Second sample with gaps and NULL closes

solution.referenceSolution:
WITH sr AS (
  SELECT security_id, price_date,
         close * 1.0 / LAG(close) OVER (PARTITION BY security_id ORDER BY price_date) - 1 AS ret
  FROM DailyPrices WHERE close IS NOT NULL
),
br AS (
  SELECT sector, bench_date,
         bench_close * 1.0 / LAG(bench_close) OVER (PARTITION BY sector ORDER BY bench_date) - 1 AS ret
  FROM Benchmarks WHERE bench_close IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT sr.security_id, m.sector,
       COUNT(*) AS days,
       ROUND(AVG(sr.ret - br.ret), 6) AS avg_excess,
       SUM(CASE WHEN sr.ret > br.ret THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS days_outperformed
FROM sr
JOIN SectorMap m ON m.security_id = sr.security_id
JOIN br ON br.sector = m.sector AND br.bench_date = sr.price_date
WHERE sr.ret IS NOT NULL AND br.ret IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY sr.security_id, m.sector
ORDER BY avg_excess DESC, sr.security_id ASC;
solution.explanation: Two CTEs compute returns with LAG over the NULL-filtered rows of each series (partitioned by security and by sector). Joining them on sector/date and averaging the difference gives the requested statistics; windows must be computed before the join so the neighbouring row is the previous *available* observation.

questions.title: Carry Forward Missing Closes
questions.statement:
Repair missing closing prices in `DailyPrices` by **carrying forward**: for every row whose `close` is NULL, set `close` to the `close` of the **most recent earlier row (smaller `price_date`) of the same security that has a non-NULL close**.

Rows with no earlier non-NULL close must stay NULL. Rows that already have a close, and all other columns and tables, must not change. A run of several consecutive NULL days all receive the same carried-forward value.

tables.name: DailyPrices
tables.description: One row per security per trading date.

questions.outputSpec: Final contents of DailyPrices (all columns) plus Securities, SectorMap and Benchmarks must match the expected state.

checkQueries.sql: SELECT * FROM DailyPrices ORDER BY security_id, price_date
SELECT * FROM Benchmarks ORDER BY sector, bench_date
SELECT * FROM Securities ORDER BY security_id

solution.referenceSolution:
UPDATE DailyPrices
SET close = (SELECT p2.close
             FROM DailyPrices p2
             WHERE p2.security_id = DailyPrices.security_id
               AND p2.price_date  < DailyPrices.price_date
               AND p2.close IS NOT NULL
             ORDER BY p2.price_date DESC
             LIMIT 1)
WHERE close IS NULL
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM DailyPrices p3
              WHERE p3.security_id = DailyPrices.security_id
                AND p3.price_date < DailyPrices.price_date
                AND p3.close IS NOT NULL);
solution.explanation: A correlated scalar subquery with ORDER BY price_date DESC LIMIT 1 over earlier non-NULL rows of the same security returns the latest valid close; if none exists it returns NULL, which is exactly the required behaviour for leading gaps (the extra EXISTS only avoids pointless writes). Carry-forward is idempotent, so the order in which rows are updated does not matter.

questions.title: Weekly Summary with Friday Week Ends
questions.statement:
Daily prices (including occasional weekend prints) must be summarised into weeks that **end on Friday**. Implement `weekly_summary(prices)`.

1. Parse `date` and drop rows with a missing `close`.
2. Define `week_end` as the first Friday on or after the date (Friday → itself, Saturday/Sunday → the following Friday, Monday → the Friday of that week).
3. Group by `symbol` and `week_end`, ordering rows within a group by `date` (stable). Compute `close_last` (close of the latest date), `volume_sum`, `high_close`, `low_close` and `n_days` (rows in the week).
4. Weeks without data do not appear. Return `symbol, week_end, close_last, volume_sum, high_close, low_close, n_days` sorted by `symbol`, `week_end`; default index.

publicTests.description: Sample: weekend prints roll into the next Friday week; NaN close dropped

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd

def weekly_summary(prices):
    df = prices.copy()
    df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
    df = df.dropna(subset=["close"])
    df = df.sort_values(["symbol", "date"], kind="mergesort")
    df["week_end"] = df["date"] + pd.to_timedelta((4 - df["date"].dt.weekday) % 7, unit="D")
    out = (df.groupby(["symbol", "week_end"], as_index=False)
             .agg(close_last=("close", "last"), volume_sum=("volume", "sum"),
                  high_close=("close", "max"), low_close=("close", "min"), n_days=("close", "size")))
    return out.sort_values(["symbol", "week_end"]).reset_index(drop=True)
solution.explanation: Compute week_end with ((4 - weekday) % 7) days offset (equivalent to resample('W-FRI')), sort by date so first/last aggregations are well-defined, then groupby-agg with named aggregations.

questions.title: Rolling Metrics on a Business-Day Calendar
questions.statement:
Price series often have missing days. Implement `rolling_metrics(prices)`.

For each `symbol` (processed independently, symbols in ascending order):

1. Parse `date`; sort by date and, if a date appears more than once, keep the **last** row.
2. Re-index to **every business day (Mon–Fri)** from the symbol's first to last date (`freq='B'`). Weekend rows are discarded.
3. `was_missing` = the close is missing (NaN or newly inserted) **before** filling.
4. Forward-fill `close`, filling **at most 2 consecutive** missing days (`limit=2`); longer gaps stay NaN after the second filled day.
5. `ret = close / previous_row_close - 1` on the filled close (NaN if either is NaN).
6. `ma5` = rolling mean of the filled close over 5 rows and `vol5` = rolling sample standard deviation (ddof = 1) of `ret` over 5 rows; both need a full window of 5 non-NaN values (`min_periods=5`).

Return `symbol, date, close, was_missing, ret, ma5, vol5`, symbols ascending then dates ascending, default index. An empty input gives an empty frame with those columns.

def rolling_metrics(prices: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = prices.copy()
    # TODO
    return df

comparison.dtypePolicy: Values compared by category: numeric (int/float interchangeable), bool, datetime, str; nulls (NaN/NaT/None/pd.NA) equal each other.

publicTests.description: Sample: missing business days, NaN, weekend row, forward-fill limit
Duplicates keep last; gap longer than the fill limit

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd

COLS = ["symbol", "date", "close", "was_missing", "ret", "ma5", "vol5"]

def rolling_metrics(prices):
    df = prices.copy()
    df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
    frames = []
    for sym, g in df.groupby("symbol", sort=True):
        s = (g.sort_values("date", kind="mergesort").drop_duplicates("date", keep="last")
              .set_index("date")["close"])
        idx = pd.date_range(s.index.min(), s.index.max(), freq="B")
        s = s.reindex(idx)
        was_missing = s.isna().to_numpy()
        c = s.ffill(limit=2)
        ret = c / c.shift(1) - 1
        frames.append(pd.DataFrame({
            "symbol": sym, "date": idx, "close": c.to_numpy(), "was_missing": was_missing, "ret": ret.to_numpy(),
            "ma5": c.rolling(5, min_periods=5).mean().to_numpy(), "vol5": ret.rolling(5, min_periods=5).std().to_numpy()}))
    if not frames:
        return pd.DataFrame({"symbol": pd.Series([], dtype=object), "date": pd.Series([], dtype="datetime64[ns]"), "close": pd.Series([], dtype="float64"),
                             "was_missing": pd.Series([], dtype=bool), "ret": pd.Series([], dtype="float64"), "ma5": pd.Series([], dtype="float64"), "vol5": pd.Series([], dtype="float64")})
    return pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)[COLS]
solution.explanation: Per symbol: sort/dedupe, reindex to a business-day range, record was_missing, ffill(limit=2), compute returns by division with shift(1) and rolling(5, min_periods=5) statistics. Rolling windows count rows, not calendar days, so inserting the missing business days first matters.

questions.title: IQR Outlier Capping per Symbol
questions.statement:
Implement `clip_outliers(returns)` which caps extreme returns separately for each symbol.

For each `symbol`, with `q1` and `q3` the 25th and 75th percentiles of its non-NaN `ret` (pandas default linear interpolation) and `iqr = q3 - q1`, the fences are `lo = q1 - 1.5*iqr` and `hi = q3 + 1.5*iqr`.

* Symbols with fewer than 4 non-NaN returns are **not** processed: `ret_clipped = ret` and `is_outlier = False`.
* Otherwise `ret_clipped = ret` clipped to `[lo, hi]` and `is_outlier` is `True` exactly when `ret < lo` or `ret > hi`. NaN returns stay NaN with `is_outlier = False`.

Keep the original row order and return `symbol, date, ret, ret_clipped, is_outlier` with default index.
questions.starterCode:
import pandas as pd

def clip_outliers(returns: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = returns.copy()
    # TODO
    return df
questions.outputSpec: Columns [symbol str, date str, ret float64, ret_clipped float64, is_outlier bool], original row order preserved.

comparison.dtypePolicy: Values compared by category: numeric (int/float interchangeable), bool, datetime, str; nulls (NaN/NaT/None/pd.NA) equal each other.

publicTests.description: Sample: outlier flagged, NaN kept, small group untouched
Constant series: IQR 0 and no outliers

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd

def clip_outliers(returns):
    df = returns.copy()
    q1 = df.groupby("symbol")["ret"].transform(lambda s: s.quantile(0.25))
    q3 = df.groupby("symbol")["ret"].transform(lambda s: s.quantile(0.75))
    n = df.groupby("symbol")["ret"].transform("count")
    lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * (q3 - q1), q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1)
    active = n >= 4
    df["ret_clipped"] = df["ret"].where(~active, df["ret"].clip(lower=lo, upper=hi))
    df["is_outlier"] = (active & ((df["ret"] < lo) | (df["ret"] > hi))).astype(bool)
    return df[["symbol", "date", "ret", "ret_clipped", "is_outlier"]].reset_index(drop=True)
solution.explanation: groupby().transform with quantile broadcasts the per-symbol statistics back to the rows, so the original order is kept; Series.clip(lower, upper) takes aligned Series bounds, and boolean masks produce the flag.

questions.title: Maximum Profit from Non-Overlapping Trade Windows
questions.statement: A desk can run at most one strategy at a time. Each candidate strategy is `[start, end, profit]`, occupying the half-open interval `[start, end)` – a strategy may start exactly when another ends. Choose a set of strategies with no overlaps that maximises total profit and return that maximum.

hiddenTests.description: One huge job beats many small

solution.referenceSolution:
from bisect import bisect_right
from typing import List

def max_profit(jobs: List[List[int]]) -> int:
    jobs = sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j[1])
    ends = [j[1] for j in jobs]
    best = [0] * (len(jobs) + 1)              # best[i] = optimum using the first i jobs (by end time)
    for i, (s, e, p) in enumerate(jobs, 1):
        k = bisect_right(ends, s, 0, i - 1)    # number of jobs finishing at or before s
        best[i] = max(best[i - 1], best[k] + p)
    return best[-1]
solution.explanation: Weighted interval scheduling. Sort by end time; best[i] = max(best[i-1], profit_i + best[k]) where k is the number of jobs ending at or before start_i, found with bisect_right on the sorted end times.
